statement: Whenever remove_interval returns a result r, r is exactly the following concatenation, in increasing i for i = 0,1,...,n-1, of piece lists P_i. If b <= s_i or a >= e_i, then P_i is the single interval [s_i,e_i]. Otherwise P_i is the concatenation of [s_i,a] (included exactly when s_i < a) followed by [b,e_i] (included exactly when b < e_i). Empty P_i contributes nothing. Every interval [u,v) is represented by the two-element vector [u,v]. Thus the represented set is the input set with toBeRemoved removed; additionally, if a = b lies strictly inside some input interval [s_i,e_i), that interval is split at a into [s_i,a) and [a,e_i), matching the stated empty-removal case.
preconditions: Let n = len(intervals). intervals has n >= 1 elements; every intervals[i] has length exactly 2, and with s_i = intervals[i][0], e_i = intervals[i][1] we have -10^9 <= s_i < e_i <= 10^9 for 0 <= i < n, and e_i <= s_{i+1} for 0 <= i < n-1 (sorted disjoint half-open intervals). toBeRemoved has length exactly 2; with a = toBeRemoved[0], b = toBeRemoved[1], we have a <= b.

statement: Whenever remove_interval returns a result r, every returned interval has one of three origins. For every j with 0 <= j < len(r), writing c = r[j][0] and d = r[j][1], there exists i with 0 <= i < n such that at least one of the following holds: (i) c = s_i, d = e_i, and (b <= s_i or a >= e_i); (ii) c = s_i, d = a, and s_i < a < e_i; (iii) c = b, d = e_i, and s_i < b < e_i.
